title: Family The Industrialization of the Remote Mind Sancho, Norma
author: Sancho, Norma
summary: Norma Sancho writes a sharp critique of distance education from the student's perspective, arguing that the promise of 'learning from anywhere' has in practice delivered an industrialized content-delivery apparatus that mistakes access to files and recorded videos for actual education. Sancho argues that a student who enrolls in a distance program has reasonable expectations: a teacher on the other side of the screen, a community of learners, feedback on their work, and some evidence that the institution understands the difference between uploading content and educating a person. Instead, most distance students receive automated quizzes, unread forum threads, and a credential waiting at the end of a sequence of self-guided activities. The article traces distance education's historical promises and argues the gap between those promises and current practice represents a structural failure to take seriously what learning -- as opposed to credentialing -- actually requires.
points: A student who pays for distance education has reasonable and non-naive expectations of meaningful guidance, genuine feedback, and evidence of human engagement -- not access to a file repository and an automated quiz sequence.

Distance education has been structurally captured by the economics of scalability: the marginal cost of adding a student to an existing course approaches zero, creating institutional incentives to maximize enrollment and minimize human instructional contact.

Forum discussions and automated feedback loops cannot substitute for the responsive, adaptive feedback of a human instructor who reads a student's specific work and addresses the specific gap -- which is what most learning actually requires.

The credential that waits at the end of a distance sequence certifies completion, not learning -- a distinction that matters enormously when the credential is used as a signal of competence in professional contexts.

Sancho's critique applies not only to purely online institutions but to 'blended' and 'hybrid' versions of residential education that increasingly look like distance education dressed in campus clothing.
quotes: Help Norma get a laptop, and pay for rent, food and basic necessities, or become a paying subscriber, or make her a job offer. [ ] When a person decides to study at a distance, she does not imagine herself entering social media. Not the old school, of course, not the classroom with its rows of desks, its hallway noise, its clock on the wall and its teacher standing in front of bodies gathered at the same hour, but still school, some recognizable form of it.
